I have managed subcontractors for fifteen years, and I have learned one thing: a firm complaint is not an angry complaint. When a crew is a no-show, I call the owner of the company the same day. I say three things. First, the fact: your crew was supposed to start at seven, and nobody came. Second, the impact: the pour on Thursday depends on that work. Third, what I need, and by when. I never shout, and I never make a threat that I am not ready to carry out. Then I put everything in writing, the same afternoon. Some people think an email is cold. It is not. It is the only thing anybody remembers three months later, when the lawyers read the file.

I run a small roofing company in Ohio, so I have been on the other side of these calls many times. The worst call I ever got was from a general contractor who shouted at me for ten minutes. I hung up, and honestly, I did not want to go back to that job. The best call was from a project manager who said: your crew was supposed to be here on Monday, and I need to know what happened. Then she listened. She gave me a grace period of forty-eight hours and asked for a recovery plan. She also told me that, unless we were on site by Wednesday, she would bring in another crew. She was firm, and she was fair. We were there on Wednesday at six in the morning, and I still work with her today.
